95	### Merging a stack — what actually happens (learned 2026-09-17, twice)
96	
97	**`gh pr merge` refuses a stacked pull request**, and on the top of a stack it silently merges into the parent branch instead of `main`. Never use it on a stack. Merge **bottom-up** through the async route; `plans/scripts/land.sh <pr> "<title>" <message-file>` does the waiting and polling:
98	
99	```bash
100	gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async -f merge_method=squash \
101	  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" -f commit_message="<the What, as prose>" -f sha=<head sha>
102	gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>      # poll until "merged"
103	```
104	
105	After a parent merges:
106	
107	1. **A linear child is restacked by GitHub itself** within about half a minute: rebased onto `main`, base retargeted to `main`. Your local copy of that branch is now behind a rewritten remote — check the trees are identical (`git diff --quiet origin/<b> <b>`) and `git reset --hard origin/<b>`. Then wait for checks and merge.
108	2. **A child carrying merge commits is not restacked.** Two cases:
109	   - *It is a strict superset of `main`* (it merged its parents in as they were first written). Prove it — the merged pull requests' original tips are ancestors, and `git diff --stat origin/main HEAD` lists only this pull request's files. A plain `git merge origin/main` will conflict on every file both sides touched (add/add against the squashed copies), so record the merge with `git merge -s ours origin/main`, confirm the tree did not change, push, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
110	   - *It is not a superset* (main moved for other reasons). `git rebase --onto origin/main <old-parent-tip> <branch>`, confirm `git diff --stat <reviewed-tip> HEAD -- <your dirs>` is empty, `git push --force-with-lease`, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
111	3. **Run a join check before merging the second of two parallel stacks**: both test suites and the end-to-end test on the rebased top branch. In stack 03 it caught an end-to-end assertion that typed in a fixture number the other stack had changed.
112	4. **After changing a pull request's base by hand, GitHub can keep a stale `CONFLICTING` and schedule no checks at all** (stack 04, #39): confirm `gh pr view <n> --json mergeable` is `MERGEABLE` and that `gh pr checks <n>` lists jobs BEFORE waiting on them; if not, `gh pr close <n> && gh pr reopen <n>` makes it recompute and run CI. GitHub also did not restack a child whose branch had been force-pushed — use the `rebase --onto` route above and prove the tree is identical to the reviewed tip.
113	5. Afterwards: delete branches locally and with `gh api -X DELETE repos/kgang/katalyst/git/refs/heads/<branch>`, `git worktree remove` each worktree, `git fetch --prune`. Leave the `entire/*` branches alone — they are the checkpoint tool's.

## What

Nine things a reviewer meets before they have decided anything. No domain change, no schema change, no new concept — one browser branch off the growing map.

**A mouse can reach the thing this product is for.** The panel of operations had exactly two ways in: the `E` key and a command in the palette. Somebody working the screen by pointing at things could click every tile, read the whole argument, find no verb anywhere on it and conclude the tool is a viewer. The Inspector's head now carries the way in — **Change this claim** on a claim, **Change this push** on an arrow — in the vocabulary's own words, as a word with a hairline round it. It is in the panel's head rather than on the tile because a tile's height is reserved before the browser has drawn one, so a new row on a tile lays the whole map out again. It is handed over only while the operations are shut: a way in that is already in is not a control, and on an arrow a second one would put two buttons reading *Change this push* on one screen.

**The two operations that are easiest to confuse say the difference before the press.** *Suppose this is true* and *This happened* both fix a claim's value and differ in what else may move. That was spoken only after the click, by which time the reader has chosen. Each now carries the shared vocabulary's own meaning as a subtitle, word for word from the *Interface words* table.

**Nothing on the panel takes a press and then explains that it cannot act.** *Split this claim · not yet built* is gone until it is built. Its words stay settled in the vocabulary and what it would do stays written in the interventions chapter.

**The change list leads with its rows.** The heading used to be followed by a four-or-five-line summary and a three-line methodology note: seven lines of prose between a reader and the one artefact that answers *what did my edit do, ranked*. The rows come first, the note is the caption it already read like, and the summary closes. Ranked against unranked, the *no change* row and the reason line are untouched.

**The map read as a list is one sentence wide again.** An outline item was a two-column grid, `2.4em 1fr`, whose first column held a claim letter that was taken off every surface when identifiers stopped being printed. The track stayed, and a grid puts its one remaining child in the first track — so every sentence was wrapping inside two and a half characters. One column now, floored at zero.

**Two rules that said the opposite of the rule in force are deleted.** `.branch-panel`'s `max-height: 28%` and `overflow-y: auto`, and `.intervene`'s `overflow-y: auto`. `.page--map .dock > *` is two classes to their one and already won with `max-height: none; overflow: visible`.
